title: Trump Says the Border Is Secure. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott Keeps Declaring an Emergency.
author: Lexi Churchill
content:
Last month, [Texas Gov. Greg Abbott](https://directory.texastribune.org/greg-
abbott/) repeated a claim he’s made for the past five years. He stated that
the number of people crossing the Texas-Mexico border illegally “posed an
ongoing and imminent threat” across the state. In doing so, he renewed a
border security disaster proclamation that has greatly expanded his powers
without going through the state Legislature.

Abbott’s declaration stands in sharp contrast to the numbers reported by the
Trump administration, which says the drop in the flow of migrants crossing the
border has been unprecedented and has [reached historic
lows](https://www.cbp.gov/newsroom/national-media-release/trump-
administration-delivers-16-straight-months-zero-releases) since it took over
in January 2025.

Yet, since Abbott first declared an emergency at the border during the Biden
administration in 2021, [he’s renewed or amended the
proclamation](https://gov.texas.gov/uploads/files/press/DISASTER_border_security_renewal_proc_IMAGE_09-14-2026.pdf)
at least 69 times — 21 of those during Trump’s tenure.

The Republican governor, who is running for his fourth term next month, has
[consolidated power like no Texas
governor](https://www.propublica.org/article/greg-abbotts-executive-power-
play) before him, building on his predecessors’ efforts to strengthen what by
design is supposed to be a “weak governor” state as the constitution limits
what can be done without legislative approval, ProPublica and The Texas
Tribune have reported. One of the methods he’s used to do that is issuing
executive orders and disaster declarations that allow him to shift funds,
suspend regulations and award no-bid contracts at times of emergency.

Since January 2025, two of the top agencies involved with border enforcement —
the Department of Public Safety and the Texas Military Department — have
awarded more than $5 million in noncompetitive contracts citing the emergency
for items like a Ford F-150, rifles and apartments, state records show.

“I think it’s unprecedented,” said Cal Jillson, a political science professor
at Southern Methodist University in Dallas. “I don’t think that there is a
similar example, certainly not as to the length of the emergency, and
certainly not after the emergency has seemed to pass.”

Abbott’s office did not respond to specific questions for this story,
including about the noncompetitive contracts, but Deputy Press Secretary
Madeline Waschak said in a written statement that the governor has been clear
that border security is an ongoing priority.

“The damage caused by four years of failed border policies under Democrat rule
did not disappear overnight, and the progress we have made will not sustain
itself without continued vigilance,” she wrote.

“Securing the border requires constant, deliberate action to combat illegal
crossings, cartel smuggling, fentanyl trafficking, and other criminal activity
that threatens public safety in Texas. Governor Abbott will ensure the tools
remain in place to safeguard our state as we work alongside the Trump
Administration to deter, arrest, detain, and deport illegal immigrants,” she
added.

At the time of Abbott’s first border declaration, four months into President
Joe Biden’s term, Border Patrol was [making more than 180,000
apprehensions](https://www.cbp.gov/newsroom/national-media-release/cbp-
announces-may-2021-operational-update) along the southwest border in a single
month. According to Abbott, the federal government’s inability or
unwillingness to enforce immigration laws had created a humanitarian crisis in
many communities in Texas.

“The Biden Administration’s open-border policies have enabled escalating
violence from the cartels, dramatically increased the risk of human
trafficking, and created a severe crisis of illegal drugs crossing into the
United States,” [the order
stated](https://gov.texas.gov/uploads/files/press/DISASTER_border_security_IMAGE_05-31-2021.pdf).

Since then, apprehensions along the southwest border have dropped on average
to about 8,000 a month this year.

The border security declaration remains Abbott’s longest continuously running
emergency proclamation. Abbott similarly renewed his 2020 COVID-19 disaster
declaration for three years, even as he downplayed the severity of the
pandemic.

“This is the quiet power of the governor,” said Brandon Rottinghaus, a
professor of political science at the University of Houston. “It’s not
something often that they brag about because the more that it becomes a
political issue, the more that there might be some contestation of it.”

Other than border security, the governor’s second longest-running emergency
declaration is related to droughts. He declared a state disaster in July 2022
and within days amended it bringing the total of counties to 189. He’s
continued to renew it, but now it applies to about a third of the counties
originally identified.

State lawmakers have repeatedly tried — and failed — to curb the governor’s
powers under the state’s disaster act. Last year, legislators from both
parties filed at least a handful of measures that would mandate Abbott get
approval from the Legislature if he wanted to extend a disaster declaration,
but none passed.

Abbott’s emergency declarations have been accompanied by record spending on
border security efforts. Texas budgeted over $11 billion during the Biden
administration and allotted an additional $3 billion last year, after Trump
took office.

It’s all part of Abbott’s Operation Lone Star, an initiative he launched in
March 2021 contending it was needed to stem the smuggling of drugs and people
into the country through Texas. Because of the emergency declaration, police
could charge immigrants with criminal trespassing for crossing the border
through private property, and the governor was able to shift money from other
agencies to fund the operation and build border barriers, deploy the National
Guard and get help from other states.

Much of the funding for Operation Lone Star is funneled through the Texas
Military Department and DPS, two of the agencies responsible for major
enforcement efforts. But the governor’s share of border spending has also
ballooned since Abbott took office over a decade ago. State lawmakers allotted
his office nearly $230 million last year to distribute through grants, largely
to local prosecutors and government agencies helping the state with Operation
Lone Star.

Though the situation on the ground has changed, one aspect of the emergency
declaration has remained constant: the ability of state agencies to award
noncompetitive contracts.

DPS and the Texas Military Department have awarded at least six noncompetitive
contracts so far during the second Trump administration for work related to
the operation where they cite an emergency. This includes a more than $2
million contract to Texas-based CTC Gunworks LLC for rifles and pistols for
active-duty personnel. CTC Gunworks officials could not be reached for
comment.

Officials with the Texas Military Department referred questions about its
procurement process to the governor’s office. A DPS spokesperson said in a
written statement that even though the disaster declaration allows for
expedited purchases, the department still follows best practices and “aims to
select vendors offering the best value, determined by cost, quality, and
ability to meet the specific disaster response requirements.”

Regarding the specific contracts, the DPS spokesperson said they were
purchases tied to existing state contracts.

The continued funding and expansion of Operation Lone Star has come even as
it’s been plagued with problems. In 2022, an [investigation by ProPublica, the
Tribune and The Marshall Project](https://www.propublica.org/series/billions-
on-the-border) found that the state’s reported success included arrests
unrelated to the border or immigration and counted drug seizures made by
troopers from across the state who were not directly assigned to the
operation. [The Tribune](https://www.texastribune.org/2022/01/07/texas-border-
national-guard-pay-suicides/) and [Army
Times](https://www.armytimes.com/news/your-army/2021/12/23/wave-of-suicides-
hits-texas-national-guards-border-mission/) also exposed poor working
conditions, pay delays and suicides among National Guard members deployed as
part of Operation Lone Star.

During a Tribune-hosted event this week with state lawmakers from El Paso,
Democratic state [Rep. Mary González](https://directory.texastribune.org/mary-
e-gonzalez/), vice chair of the Appropriations Committee, said state
legislators have already started to scale back when it comes to border funding
and there’s interest from both sides of the aisle to continue to do so in the
upcoming legislative session.

“I think that the problem is that some of that border security money still
lies in the governor’s office which has no checks and balances and because we
are still under an emergency — which is not an emergency anymore — an
emergency border security statement which he can just use that money, you have
seen some questionable appropriations under the veil of border security,” she
said.

Abbott, however, has repeatedly said that Texas’ work in securing the border
is not over.

“We must secure the border not just for the next two years of the Trump
administration, but we gotta do it forever,” Abbott said at a [press
conference in early October](https://www.c-span.org/program/public-affairs-
event/tx-gov-abbott-r-signs-proclamation-on-border-security-
reimbursement/686014) where he discussed the federal government’s $7.5 billion
reimbursement for border security expenses the state had incurred.

Rottinghaus said that Texas will always have to confront border crossings and
drug trafficking, but the existence of those problems don’t always justify an
emergency declaration.

“Even someone who strongly supports the governor’s board of policies might ask
whether they want a future governor of the opposite party using the same
interpretation of emergency authority for years,” Rottinghaus said, adding
that the issue is that “governors, once they get a power, are hesitant to give
it back.”

Declaring an Emergency.](https://www.propublica.org/article/greg-abbott-
